Brand elements: name, logo, colors, tagline
What a brand does: identifies, differentiates, builds expectations
Brand and trust: a brand as a shortcut for expectations

claims.claim: A brand is any distinctive feature - a name, term, design, or symbol - that identifies a seller's goods or services; the working definition used in this lesson adds that this feature distinguishes one seller's offering from competitors'.
The classic brand elements include the name, the logo, colors, and the tagline; the AMA lists a brand's name, logo, and color scheme among the visual and symbolic elements of brand identity.

A brand identifies the seller, differentiates the offering from competitors, and builds customer expectations; the AMA describes brand marketing as creating a unique identity and perceptions that differentiate a brand from competitors.

Brand trust is the faith consumers place in a brand; a positive brand image fosters trust, loyalty, and repeat purchases, which supports the lesson's framing of a brand as a shortcut for expectations.

Brand identity is the expression of a brand assembled by its owner - name, logo, visual appearance, communications - reflecting how the owner wants consumers to perceive it; brand image is the customer's mental picture, formed by experience.
While marketing teams can influence how a brand is seen, consumers often define the brand; the brand is an intangible asset made up of the organization's promotion efforts plus consumer meaning.
Building a strong brand is a discipline of consistency over time: every product, promotion, and event must reinforce the brand, building value gradually.
Brand equity - the value a brand holds in the minds of consumers, or the additional value a brand has over a substitute - is a distinct concept covered by its own sibling topic, not by this lesson.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Wording of the brand definition: the AMA topic page currently reads 'a brand is any distinctive feature like a name, term, design, or symbol that identifies goods or services,' while the longer classic definition (reflected in Wikipedia's article and in USPTO trademark language quoted by OpenStax) adds that the feature distinguishes one seller's goods or service from those of other sellers.
positions: AMA short form: identifies goods or services
Classic long form: identifies and distinguishes one seller from others
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson uses the combined working definition - a name, term, design, or symbol, or a combination, that identifies a seller's offering and distinguishes it from competitors - attributed to the AMA, which is consistent with both phrasings.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Brand identity and brand image are sometimes used interchangeably in casual business writing, and some sources treat 'brand identity' as only the visual system (logo, colors, typography).
positions: Narrow view: brand identity equals the visual/symbolic elements (AMA topic page phrasing)
Standard marketing view: brand identity is the full owner-projected expression, distinct from the customer-perceived brand image (Wikipedia, OpenStax)
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches the standard distinction - identity is what the company projects, image is what customers perceive - while still naming the visible elements (name, logo, colors, tagline) as the carriers of identity, so both views are honored.

The draft's toolbox-drawer analogy ('a label on a toolbox drawer') - generic boilerplate with no source support; replaced with an original restaurant-sign analogy.
The draft's claim that context and evidence are the central ideas of branding - not supported by any marketing source; the lesson instead teaches brand elements, functions, and identity-versus-image.

sourceRecords.notes: Tier D reputable reference, read live 2026-08-22. Corroborates the classic AMA definition (a name, term, design, symbol, or other feature that distinguishes one seller's goods or service from others); lists brand elements including name, logo, tagline or catchphrase, and colors; and states the identity-versus-image distinction (identity is owner-assembled and reflects how the owner wants the brand perceived; image is the customer's mental picture) and the brand-trust concept (faith of consumers; positive image fosters loyalty and repeat purchases).
